name.text: MQH - Evaluating Improper Integrals with a point of discontinuity

questiontext.text:
Evaluate the integral below and determine if it converges or diverges.

Note: \( \infty\) is entered as inf \( -\infty\) is entered as minf and \( \sqrt{a}\) is entered as sqrt(a).

\(\displaystyle \int_{{@lower_lm@}}^{{@upper_lm@}} {@fx@} \,dx=\) [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

Therefore, the integral is [[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]] [[feedback:prt2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Worked solution

To determine whether the integral

\(\displaystyle \int_{{@lower_lm@}}^{{@upper_lm@}} {@fx@} \,dx\)

is improper, we need to examine the integrand \( \displaystyle {@fx@}\).

Step \(1\): Check for Impropriety

The function \( \displaystyle {@fx@}\) is defined as long as \({@uu@} > 0\), which means \(x < {@point_disc@}\). At \(x = {@point_disc@}\), the integrand becomes undefined because it leads to division by zero. Therefore, the upper limit of the integral is a point of discontinuity.

Since the integral has an endpoint where the integrand is undefined, it is an improper integral.

Step \(2\): Determine Convergence or Divergence of the integral

To analyze the convergence or divergence of the integral, we can express it as a limit.

Therefore, we’ll need to replace the point of discontinuity which is the upper limit \(({@point_disc@})\) with a parameter \(t\) as follows,

\( \displaystyle \int_{{@lower_lm@}}^{{@upper_lm@}} {@fx@} \, dx = \lim_{t \to {@point_disc@}^-} \int_{@lower_lm@}^t {@fx@}\, dx\)

Step \(3\): Evaluate the Integral

Now we will evaluate the integral \(\displaystyle \int_{@lower_lm@}^t {@fx@}\, dx\).

To do this, we can use substitution.

Let:

\( \qquad \displaystyle u = {@uu@} \implies du = {@del_dx@}\)

\(\quad \, \, \) When \(x = {@lower_lm@}\), \(u = {@u1@}\), and when \(x = t\), \(u = {@u2@}\). Thus, we rewrite the integral:

\(\qquad \displaystyle \int_{@lower_lm@}^t {@fx@}\, dx = \int_{@u1@}^{@u2@}{@fu@}\, du \)


Evaluating this integral:

\( \qquad \displaystyle \int {@fu@} \, du = {@new_indef@}+ C\)

So we have:

\(\qquad \begin{align} \displaystyle\int_{@u1@}^{@u2@} {@fu@} \, du & = \Bigg[ {@new_indef@} \Bigg]_{{@u1@}}^{@u2@} \\ &={@upper@} - {@lower@} \\ &= {@indef_val@} \end{align}\)

Now we need to take the limit as \(t \to {@point_disc@}^- ,\) as \(t\) approaches \({@point_disc@}^- , \displaystyle {@den@}\) approaches \(0\):

\( \qquad \displaystyle \lim_{t \to {@point_disc@}^-} \Bigg( {@indef_val@} \Bigg) = {@result@}\)

The improper integral is {@mcq_correct(ta_4)[1]@}, and its exact value is \(\displaystyle \boxed{{@result@}} \).

hint.text:
Start by looking at the integrand \( \displaystyle {@fx@} \).

Notice that the denominator involves a square root. For the integrand to be well-defined, the expression under the square root, \( {@b*point_disc - b*x@} \), must be positive.

If it equals zero, the function becomes undefined. So, check for values of \(x\) that could cause this to happen, and focus on the limits of the integral.

Since the square root function has a potential issue when \( {@b*point_disc - b*x@} = 0 \) (i.e., \(x = {@upper_lm@}\)), we need to carefully evaluate the integral near this point.

This suggests that the integral might be improper.
To handle this, we rewrite the integral as a limit where we approach \( x = {@upper_lm@} \) from the left. This will help us analyze whether the integral converges or diverges by taking the limit as \(x\) approaches \({@upper_lm@}\).
